newsitem.title: USA: Dissidents see Deng death yielding power struggle.
newsitem.headline: Dissidents see Deng death yielding power struggle.

text.p: Two of the student leaders of the pro-democracy movement who managed to reach the United States after the 1989 Tiananmen Square uprising said on Wednesday that the death of Deng Xiaoping would have a profound effect on China.

"I know that most people tend to think that his death doesn't have an effect on China or U.S. relations. But I think that is just frustration talking," said Shen Tong, who fled China after the Tiananmen Square student revolt was crushed by the army on June 4, 1989. He arrived in the United States on June 10.
"This is the end of the first generation of the communists in China. There is no one else who has this status. Jiang Zemin has been consolidating power, but he does not have the stature," Shen said.
Jiang, whom Deng named as his successor, was swept to the top of China's leadership when hardliners toppled Zhao Ziyang after Tiananmen.
"It (Deng's death) will have a profound effect on the bureaucracies that are left over," said Shen. "What the effect will be precisely is impossible to say, but it will produce something.

"The struggle has been modified," Shen said. "China has been a totalitarian regime under the Communist Party. But now it will no longer be a situation or decision made by a single entity. Instead you will see different power centres emerge and everyone will want a piece of pie."

Wang Juntao, who China sentenced to 13 years in prison for being behind the 1989 pro-democracy movement, said from Cambridge, Massachusetts, that Deng's death before the Communist Party's national congress means there may be a power struggle ahead.

"I think that because he died before the Communist Party National conference, the political situation has more chance to change," said Wang, who was granted a medical parole in 1994 and is now a student at Harvard University.
"I think Jiang Zemin can not turn back the economic reforms. But can he still hold his power?" Wang asked. "I don't think so. I think ... other high ranking leaders will be challenging him."
Some of his political rivals include Qiao Shi, 72, chairman of the National People's Congress, or parliament, and Zhao Ziyang, analysts said.
Zhao, 77, has not been seen in public for more than six years and is believed to be under house arrest in Beijing.
